candidates.attacker_control: Primary path (OAuth2 login, default configuration): the login processing endpoint /login/oauth2/code/{registrationId} reads the request parameters error, error_description and state (OAuth2LoginAuthenticationFilter.convert, lines 193-217). error_description is copied into OAuth2AuthorizationResponse/OAuth2Error, and OAuth2Error.toString() ("[errorCode] description") becomes the message of the OAuth2AuthenticationException thrown by OAuth2LoginAuthenticationProvider when the response is an error (lines 105-108). Crucially that throw happens before the state parameter is compared (line 110), so the caller does not need to know the session's random state value; only a pending authorization request in the victim's session is required. Secondary path present in this snapshot: OpenIDAuthenticationFilter lines 128-152 include the submitted openid_identifier request parameter verbatim in the AuthenticationServiceException message. Other custom AuthenticationProvider/UserDetailsService implementations that embed request data in exception messages reach the same sink.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and excluded the possibility that the common username/password path supplies the payload: DaoAuthenticationProvider rejects null credentials and emits constant "Bad credentials" messages with hideUserNotFoundExceptions=true (default), so plain form login alone does not expose attacker text. Verified that the OAuth2 path is reachable without knowing the per-session state value because the statusError() branch precedes the state comparison; verified the filter only requires that some OAuth2AuthorizationRequest be stored in the session (lines 145-149), which an attacker can trigger with a first navigation. Verified that the failure message really lands in the session attribute and is really rendered by the login filter (single consumer of WebAttributes.AUTHENTICATION_EXCEPTION on the rendering side; SimpleUrlAuthenticationSuccessHandler clears it only on success). Verified that the same class escapes another value with HtmlUtils.htmlEscape (line 290) and that the loss of encoding is specific to errorMsg, so the omission is not compensated elsewhere. Checked that the WebFlux default login page (LoginPageGeneratingWebFilter) hard-codes "Invalid credentials" and is not a second sink. Checked that for form login the filter is installed by default (DefaultLoginPageConfigurer installs it because ExceptionHandlingConfigurer.getAuthenticationEntryPoint() is null unless explicitly set) and that the default failure URL is loginPage + "?error". Also verified that OAuth2Error/OAuth2AuthenticationException preserve the description in toString()/getMessage().
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting in the application's own origin on the authentication page. An attacker who can drive the victim's browser through the above flow can execute script in the victim's session context: read/extract session cookies or the CSRF token rendered by the same page, act as the victim, or display credential-phishing content on a trusted URL. Because the exception text stays in the session and is re-rendered at /login?error until a successful authentication clears it, the payload can be re-executed on subsequent error-page views within the same session. The flaw is in shipped library code and is reachable with the default OAuth2-login configuration; deployments that replace the login page or render the failure message with a custom template that escapes output are not affected.
candidates.prerequisites: Servlet (not WebFlux) application using Spring Security's generated default login page (no custom loginPage()) with oauth2Login() (or openidLogin()/form login) configured; for the OAuth2 path the victim's session must contain a stored OAuth2AuthorizationRequest (i.e. the victim has started an OAuth2 login at /oauth2/authorization/{registrationId}), and the victim must be induced to request the redirect URI with error=<code>&state=<non-empty>&error_description=<markup>. With oauth2Login() the default failure URL is /login?error (AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer.updateAuthenticationDefaults) and DefaultLoginPageConfigurer installs DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter, so the error message stored in the session is rendered on the next /login?error request. The message remains in the session until a successful login clears it (SimpleUrlAuthenticationSuccessHandler), so it can be re-rendered by later requests in the same session.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter.generateLoginPageHtml() takes the message of the AuthenticationException cached under WebAttributes.AUTHENTICATION_EXCEPTION (SPRING_SECURITY_LAST_EXCEPTION) in the HttpSession and appends it raw to the generated HTML (sb.append(errorMsg) at line 234) instead of HTML-encoding it, even though the same method encodes the OAuth2 client name via HtmlUtils.htmlEscape (line 290). Because Spring Security builds some AuthenticationException messages from request parameters and passes them through the default failure handler into that session attribute, the login page becomes an unencoded output sink for attacker-supplied text.
candidates.title: Unescaped authentication error message in servlet default login page allows XSS via attacker-controlled OAuth2 error_description
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker causes the victim's browser to begin an OAuth2 login (GET /oauth2/authorization/{registrationId}); OAuth2AuthorizationRequestRedirectFilter stores the authorization request (including state) in the session via HttpSessionOAuth2AuthorizationRequestRepository. 2) Victim is then sent to the app's redirect URI with attacker-chosen error/error_description/state parameters. 3) OAuth2LoginAuthenticationFilter loads the stored authorization request, converts the request into an OAuth2AuthorizationResponse.error(errorCode).errorDescription(attackerValue).state(attackerValue) (convert(), lines 193-217). 4) OAuth2LoginAuthenticationProvider sees statusError() and throws OAuth2AuthenticationException with message OAuth2Error.toString() == "[errorCode] " + attackerValue before validating state (lines 105-108, 110). 5) AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter routes the AuthenticationException to the default SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler, which stores it in the session under WebAttributes.AUTHENTICATION_EXCEPTION and redirects to /login?error (SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler lines 71-95, 105-118; default URL from AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer lines 378-384). 6) DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter matches the failure URL, reads ex.getMessage() (lines 213-221) and writes it into the page body without HTML encoding: response.getWriter().write(loginPageHtml) at line 201, with sb.append(errorMsg) at line 234. The resulting HTML executes attacker script in the application's origin. 7) The analogous OpenID path (claimedIdentity reflected into AuthenticationServiceException) reaches the same sink.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed, so the end-to-end browser behavior (parameter decoding of the crafted error_description, actual script execution in a container) is not runtime-confirmed. The exact upstream fix commit and CVE identifier were not consulted (out of scope for this review); it is possible the upstream remediation instead sanitized individual exception messages while leaving this sink, so the precise patch shape is unverified. Exploitability is configuration-dependent (oauth2Login()/openidLogin() enabled and the default login page in use) and requires attacker-driven navigation of the victim to establish the session-stored authorization request. I did not determine whether the exception attribute is removed by every container/session-management combination in this version.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting); missing output encoding of security-relevant error text

coverage_summary: Assigned tree: 2301 model-visible files (2004 Java; source root 2302 with one sensitive-name/path file filtered by the scope tool; no binaries over 5 MiB; NUL-containing files skipped from reading/searching). P1 relation index: partial — 886 of 2301 files parsed into 19507 symbols, 345 files omitted, calls/edges are name/type/arity-based candidates with no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution, so index edges were used only for navigation and every claim was re-verified in source text. Main areas actually read: crypto password encoders and factories (Delegating, NoOp, LdapSha, Md4, MessageDigest, Standard, Abstract, PasswordEncoderUtils), core authentication providers (Dao/AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider, UserDetailsRepositoryReactiveAuthenticationManager, User, MapReactiveUserDetailsService, JdbcDaoImpl/provisioning), web filters (AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter, SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler, DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter, Anonymous, RememberMe, Digest, Basic, UsernamePassword, SessionManagement, CsrfFilter, HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository, FirewalledResponse), firewall (StrictHttpFirewall, DefaultHttpFirewall), request matchers (AntPath, Regex), context/session classes, OAuth2 client login flow (filter, provider, endpoint/error types, redirect filter, configurer), OpenID filter/provider, CAS authentication provider, and the config-module defaults (FilterComparator, DefaultLoginPageConfigurer, ExceptionHandlingConfigurer, AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer, OAuth2LoginConfigurer). Not deeply reviewed: LDAP internals, messaging, taglibs, data, aspects, the bulk of WebFlux/reactive filters and the sample applications, plus large portions of test code; those areas are not claimed as covered.
limitations: Static review only: no code, tests, scanners or containers were executed; no runtime confirmation of the XSS chain, and parameter decoding/HTML parsing behavior is inferred from source and servlet semantics.
The P1 relation index is partial (886/2301 files parsed, 345 omitted) and explicitly has no data-flow, control-flow or semantic resolution; navigation facts were not treated as findings.
The upstream fix commit, changelog and CVE metadata were intentionally not consulted, so the association of this sink with any specific advisory or the exact shape of the remediation is unverified.

Exploitability of the candidate depends on deployment configuration (default login page in use, oauth2Login()/openidLogin()/custom providers enabled) and on attacker-driven navigation to create the session-stored authorization request; these conditions were reasoned about from source but not tested.
Coverage of the reactive/WebFlux stack, LDAP and CAS internals, XML namespace configuration paths and the sample applications was high-level only.

rejected_leads.lead: DelegatingPasswordEncoder.matches(null, null) returns true (crypto/.../DelegatingPasswordEncoder.java lines 190-193) combined with UserDetailsRepositoryReactiveAuthenticationManager passing authentication.getCredentials() straight to the encoder (lines 49-56) and ServerFormLoginAuthenticationConverter producing a token with a null password when the form field is missing (lines 47-52).
rejected_leads.reason: An authentication bypass would additionally require a UserDetails whose getPassword() is null; the built-in User class rejects null passwords and MapReactiveUserDetailsService clones users, so this is only reachable with a custom ReactiveUserDetailsService/user store. Conditional and unproven; not selected over the login-page XSS.

rejected_leads.lead: PasswordEncoderUtils.equals(null, null) evaluates to true because both lengths are -1 (lines 33-46).
rejected_leads.reason: No reachable caller passes both arguments as null: LdapShaPasswordEncoder.matches and Md4PasswordEncoder.matches dereference/parse encodedPassword before calling equals, and DaoAuthenticationProvider rejects null presented credentials. Latent defect without an established input path.

rejected_leads.lead: Null stored/erased password handling in DaoAuthenticationProvider / User.eraseCredentials and the reactive provider (password erased on shared UserDetails, then compared).
rejected_leads.reason: eraseCredentials() is applied to the User object in the authentication result, but the servlet provider rejects null presented credentials and built-in user services clone/restore password state; no concrete request path to a successful null-password comparison was found in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Legacy cryptographic comparisons: NoOp/LdapSha plaintext comparisons, MD5 remember-me token signature, and key.hashCode() equality in Anonymous/RememberMe providers.
rejected_leads.reason: These are long-standing documented-insecure legacy designs; no request-controlled path that yields authentication or authorization bypass was demonstrated, so they do not meet the evidence threshold for this review.

rejected_leads.lead: Request-matching/path-parsing bypasses (AntPathRequestMatcher, RegexRequestMatcher, StrictHttpFirewall, MvcRequestMatcher, URL normalization).
rejected_leads.reason: StrictHttpFirewall already rejects semicolons, encoded slash/period/backslash/percent and non-printable request URIs in this snapshot; no inconsistent normalization path exploitable for a matcher bypass was identified in the time available.

summary: This is the Spring Security core repository at version 5.0.12.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (gradle.properties; Spring Boot 2.0.8 / Spring Framework 5.0.13 BOM; copyright headers up to 2018), i.e. the 5.0.x maintenance line, ~2004 Java files across core, web, config, crypto, oauth2, openid, ldap, cas, acl, messaging, data, taglibs and samples. The strongest source-evidenced issue I found is in the servlet default login page: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter renders the AuthenticationException message from the HTTP session directly into its HTML response without output encoding (line 234), while it does encode the OAuth2 client name (line 290). In the shipped OAuth2-login flow, the authorization-response "error_description" request parameter is attached to OAuth2AuthenticationException's message by OAuth2LoginAuthenticationProvider before the state parameter is validated, the default failure handler stores that exception in the session, and the default failure URL (/login?error) causes the default login page to display it — so attacker-controlled markup can be reflected into the login page HTML (XSS). The same sink reflects other attacker-influenced exception messages present in this snapshot (e.g. the OpenID filter echoes the submitted openid_identifier into an AuthenticationServiceException). All hops were verified in source; no runtime execution was performed. Other candidate leads (reactive/WebFlux null-password handling, PasswordEncoderUtils.equals(null,null), remember-me MAC) were examined and rejected as unproven or unreachable with built-in components.
